profile.name: Robin Park
profile.tagline: I build tools that help developers understand unfamiliar code and change it without fear.
profile.bio:
I'm a fourth-year PhD candidate working at the intersection of **program analysis** and **human-computer interaction**. My research asks what developers actually need to know before they change code they didn't write, and builds tools that answer those questions automatically.

My recent work infers types for JSON-heavy codebases, explains refactorings as executable diffs, and studies how developers read code during review. Most of my tools have a live demo on this site, so you can try them on your own code.

Before my PhD I spent two years as a software engineer working on build infrastructure. I'm on the job market for research positions starting in fall 2027.

publications.title: Shapeshift: Lightweight Type Inference for JSON-Heavy Codebases
publications.venue: ACM International Conference on the Foundations of Software Engineering (FSE 2026)
publications.abstract: Large JavaScript and Python codebases pass JSON between services with little or no type information. We present Shapeshift, which infers precise structural types from example payloads and propagates them through code, producing TypeScript declarations developers can check in. On 40 open-source projects, Shapeshift recovered 91% of hand-written types.

publications.title: What Do Developers Ask When Reviewing Unfamiliar Code? A Study of 1,200 Review Comments
publications.venue: ACM CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI 2026)
publications.abstract: We qualitatively coded 1,200 code review comments from six open-source projects to understand which questions reviewers ask about code they did not write. Questions about **intent** and **impact** dominate, yet existing tools mostly answer questions about **structure**.

demos.description:
This is the inference engine from **Shapeshift** compiled for the browser. Nothing you paste leaves your machine.

### How it works

Shapeshift merges the shapes of every value it sees: two objects with different keys become one type with optional fields, and mixed arrays become unions. Try the *Union* example to see it merge records.

demos.description:
Each run happens in a fresh, locked-down container: no network, a read-only filesystem, 128 MB of memory, and a 10-second limit.

The container image is built from `examples/linter-demo` in this site's repository. Build it on the server with:

```
docker build -t phd-site-example-linter examples/linter-demo
```

## Prospective students

If you're an undergraduate at Northfield interested in developer tools research, I mentor one or two students each year through the lab's research program. Send me a short note about a tool you wish existed.
